title: Letting AI Interface with your App with MCP — Kent C Dodds
talk_summary: Kent C. Dodds argues that the missing piece for 'Jarvis'-style assistants is integrations, and that MCP provides a standard client/server protocol so any host app can dynamically discover and call tools from any service provider. The talk is mostly conceptual (history, architecture, a journaling/weather demo) with no performance or cost measurements.

takeaways.technique: Standardize internal tool exposure behind one protocol
takeaways.what_they_do: Service providers expose tools/resources/prompts via a standard MCP server; the host app creates a generic client per service and tells the LLM what is available, adding/removing capabilities dynamically.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the host application tells the LLM what services are available to it and those services can be dynamically added

takeaways.what_they_do: The host manages context and only advertises the tools relevant to the current query, rather than dumping every tool into every prompt.
takeaways.evidence_quote: this context can be managed by the host application and the LLM just knows what's available now

takeaways.technique: OAuth 2.1 auth built into the tool server
takeaways.what_they_do: The MCP server enforces authentication (OAuth 2.1) so authenticated actions like create/delete require a validated token, and the client authenticates once per session.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the MCP server has authentication built in. It's based on OOTH 2.1

takeaways.what_they_do: The server returns data in whatever format suits it (JSON), and the LLM/client reformats for the user, so servers don't need to know presentation.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the server can communicate in a way that makes a lot of sense for the server. Um, and then the client can take that as context
